messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 20
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: African
  relationship_status: Single
  occupation: Doctor
  trauma_type: Combat
  pcl5: 63

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Somatic (Breathlessness): Difficulty breathing or feeling short of breath, Auditory (Silence): Sudden or complete silence, Violence: Violence
  Memory: Blocked Before Complete: I find myself pushing the memory away before I can fully recall it, Fragmented Pieces: My memories of the event come in disconnected pieces that do not fit together, Memory Gaps: There are parts of the event that I simply cannot remember no matter how hard I try
  Negative Appraisals: Identity Loss: I feel like I don't know myself anymore, Shattered Beliefs: My beliefs about how the world works have been completely destroyed, Hypervigilance: I have to be on guard all the time

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Adebayo was only twenty years old, yet he carried the weariness of a man who had lived several lifetimes. He had come to the United States to continue the medical career that had started with such promise, but the promise now felt like a cruel joke. The man who had once sutured wounds under generator-powered lights in a field clinic now found his hands shaking when a hospital cart rattled down the hallway. He had been a doctor in a war zone, and the war had followed him into the quiet, sterile corridors of his new life.

The event itself refused to play out in his mind as a coherent story. Instead, it existed as a series of jagged, sensory shards. He remembered the thick, chalky dust filling his mouth and the acrid smell of explosives. He remembered the specific, high-pitched scream of a woman in the makeshift waiting area, a sound that was abruptly cut off. Then there was the pressure, an impossible weight on his chest after the mortar shell landed just outside the clinic wall, bringing a section of the roof down on him. He could recall the panicked, shallow gasps of his own breathing and, more terrifyingly, the fainter, rasping breaths of someone pinned nearby, a sound that gradually faded into nothing. The memory always stopped there. He could never recall how he was pulled from the rubble or the hours that followed. Whenever he tried to force the pieces together, to fill in the gaping holes in the timeline, a wall would come down in his mind, a visceral recoil that left him dizzy and nauseous. He would find himself pushing it away before the full horror could coalesce.

These fragments now dictated the terms of his existence. As a resident in a busy American hospital, his triggers were everywhere. A patient struggling with an acute asthma attack, their chest heaving, would send a phantom weight crashing down onto Adebayo’s own chest, making it impossible for him to breathe. He would feel the same suffocating panic he felt under the debris, the certainty that his lungs were collapsing. He had to excuse himself twice during resuscitations, feigning a dizzy spell, overwhelmed by a terror his colleagues couldn't possibly understand. The most unsettling trigger, however, was its opposite: silence. The chaos of the attack had been punctuated by a moment of absolute, ringing stillness after the main explosion. In that silence, the true scale of the devastation had settled in. Now, any sudden quiet—the pause after a monitor alarm is silenced, the dead air of an empty corridor on the night shift—felt menacing, a prelude to some unseen horror. He took to wearing a single earbud, playing quiet music almost constantly, just to keep the silence at bay.

He had come to believe the world was a fundamentally random and malevolent place. The belief that his role as a healer offered some form of protection, that a clinic was a sanctuary, had been obliterated in a single afternoon. Now, he saw threats everywhere. He was constantly scanning rooms, noting exits, assessing the people around him for any sign of aggression. He couldn't sit with his back to a door in the cafeteria. This constant state of alert was exhausting, a low-grade hum of dread that never switched off. He felt utterly disconnected from the confident, purposeful young man he had been before the attack. That person knew his place in the world; this new person was a stranger, a ghost haunting a life that no longer felt like his own. He would look in the mirror and feel a profound sense of alienation, as if his own reflection belonged to someone else.

Over the past few months, his world had shrunk. He turned down invitations from other residents, finding small talk impossible when his mind was always on patrol. He changed his specialization preference from emergency medicine to pathology, hoping a career among the dead would be quieter than one among the living. The breaking point came last week. During rounds, a patient’s family began shouting at each other in the hallway. The sudden, violent eruption of anger sent Adebayo backing away down the hall, his heart hammering against his ribs, a primal instinct screaming at him to find cover. His attending physician found him in a supply closet minutes later, staring blankly at a shelf of saline drips. It was the shame of that moment, the realization that he could no longer perform even the basic functions of his job, that finally brought him to therapy. He was terrified that he was permanently broken, but a small, desperate part of him hoped he could learn to live in the world again without feeling like he was still trapped in the ruins of that clinic.
